title: Improving pyelonephritis on ceftriaxone; only oral beta-lactam options remain

clinical_review.notes: Owner clinical review: cases look good.

story: A 52-year-old woman with acute pyelonephritis is on IV ceftriaxone, hospital day 3. She has been afebrile for 36 hours, is eating and drinking, and her vital signs are normal. The urine E. coli is susceptible to ceftriaxone and to cefazolin at the urinary surrogate breakpoint, but resistant to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and ciprofloxacin.

cultures.order_text: Bacteria identified in Urine by Culture

expected_findings.summary: Clinical criteria for an oral switch are met; the susceptible oral option is an oral cephalosporin the cefazolin urinary surrogate supports, such as cefpodoxime.

acceptable_answers: Switch to an oral third-generation cephalosporin the cefazolin surrogate supports (for example cefpodoxime) with optimized dosing, for a total course of about 7 days (IDSA 2025).
Continue IV ceftriaxone to complete a short course when oral therapy is not practical, documenting the reason.
Discuss with the team or infectious diseases before switching, given the very low certainty of the evidence for short non-fluoroquinolone courses.
reference_answer: Flag the patient as meeting clinical IV to PO criteria with an oral third-generation cephalosporin the cefazolin surrogate supports, such as cefpodoxime: IDSA 2025 calls this a reasonable switch after improvement on ceftriaxone, with optimized dosing and a total course of about 7 days. The finding should not present the switch as the only defensible choice.
rationale: She meets clinical switch criteria, and the only susceptible oral agents are beta-lactams. The 2011 IDSA guideline considered oral beta-lactams less effective for pyelonephritis and advised a longer course; the 2025 IDSA complicated UTI guideline supersedes it: after improvement on ceftriaxone an oral third-generation cephalosporin is a reasonable switch, with optimized dosing and 7 days total for a non-fluoroquinolone (very low certainty), and no longer course for beta-lactams. Nitrofurantoin does not reach renal tissue. It stays an ambiguous case because the evidence for short oral beta-lactam courses is limited (owner review, 2026-11-12).

citations.supports: Switch to oral therapy once improving, able to take oral medication, with an effective oral option; after improvement on ceftriaxone an oral third-generation cephalosporin is a reasonable choice; checked against IDSA's published PDF and approved by the owner, 2026-11-12.

Oral agents for complicated UTI: oral third-generation cephalosporins may be comparable to fluoroquinolones or TMP-SMX; cephalexin, amoxicillin and low-bioavailability cephalosporins only with caution and optimized dosing; checked against IDSA's published PDF and approved by the owner, 2026-11-12.

7 days of a non-fluoroquinolone rather than 10-14 days; no longer course for oral beta-lactams, though higher doses may be required; checked against IDSA's published PDF and approved by the owner, 2026-11-12.
Cefazolin as a surrogate for oral cephalosporins in urinary isolates.
Stewardship programs promoting timely IV to oral transition once criteria are met.
